product-of-three-numbers-4.name: Product of Three Numbers
product-of-three-numbers-4.statement:
You are given an integer $n$. Find three distinct integers $a, b, c$ such that $2 \le a, b, c$ and $a \cdot b \cdot c = n$, or report that it is impossible.

To make the answer unique, print the triple with $a < b < c$ that is lexicographically smallest, i.e. $a$ is as small as possible, and among those, $b$ is as small as possible.

You have to answer $t$ independent test cases.
product-of-three-numbers-4.input: The first line contains one integer $t$, the number of test cases. Each of the next $t$ lines contains one integer $n$.
product-of-three-numbers-4.output: For each test case, print "NO" if $n$ cannot be written as $a \cdot b \cdot c$ with distinct integers $a, b, c \ge 2$. Otherwise, print "YES" on one line, and on the next line print $a$, $b$ and $c$ separated by spaces, in the order described above.

anugyas-lantern-festival.name: Anugya’s Lantern Festival
anugyas-lantern-festival.statement:
Anugya is preparing lanterns for a festival. She has n lanterns in a row, and every lantern starts with brightness 1.

In one operation, Anugya chooses a lantern i $(1 ≤ i ≤ n)$ and an integer $x > 0$, and increases its brightness by $⌊a_i / x⌋$, where $a_i$ is the current brightness of lantern i. In other words, $a_i = a_i + ⌊a_i / x⌋$.

When all operations are done, the festival judges pay Anugya $c_i$ coins for every lantern i whose brightness is exactly $b_i$.

Find the maximum number of coins Anugya can earn using at most k operations.
anugyas-lantern-festival.input:
The first line contains a single integer t, the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains two integers n and k, the number of lanterns and the maximum number of operations.
The second line contains n integers $b_1, b_2, …, b_n$, the target brightness values.
The third line contains n integers $c_1, c_2, …, c_n$, the coins paid for each lantern.
anugyas-lantern-festival.output: For each test case, print one integer: the maximum number of coins Anugya can earn.
anugyas-lantern-festival.constraints:
$1 ≤ t ≤ 100$

$1 ≤ n ≤ 10^3$

$0 ≤ k ≤ 10^6$

$1 ≤ b_i ≤ 10^3$

$1 ≤ c_i ≤ 10^6$

The sum of n over all test cases does not exceed $10^3$.

powered-addition.name: Powered Addition
powered-addition.statement:
You have an array $a$ of length $n$. For every positive integer $x$, during the $x$-th second you perform the following operation:

Select some distinct indices $i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k$ between $1$ and $n$ inclusive, and add $2^{x-1}$ to each corresponding element: $a_{i_j} := a_{i_j} + 2^{x-1}$ for $j = 1, 2, \dots, k$. You may select no indices at all.

You want to make $a$ nondecreasing as fast as possible. Find the smallest number $T$ such that the array can be made nondecreasing after at most $T$ seconds.

An array is nondecreasing if $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n$.

You have to answer $t$ independent test cases.
powered-addition.input: The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases. For each test case, the first line contains an integer $n$, the length of the array. The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$.
powered-addition.output: For each test case, print the minimum number of seconds needed to make $a$ nondecreasing.
powered-addition.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 10^4$

$1 \le n \le 10^5$

$-10^9 \le a_i \le 10^9$

The sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^5$.

shrine.name: Shrine
shrine.statement:
There are $n$ models in a shop, numbered from $1$ to $n$, with sizes $s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n$.

A collector buys some of the models and arranges them in increasing order of their indices (not sizes). The arrangement is beautiful if for any two adjacent models with indices $i_j$ and $i_{j+1}$ (where $i_j < i_{j+1}$), $i_{j+1}$ is divisible by $i_j$ and $s_{i_j} < s_{i_{j+1}}$.

For example, for $6$ models with sizes $\{3, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7\}$, the collector can buy models $1, 2, 6$ and the arrangement is beautiful. An arrangement with exactly one model is also beautiful.

Find the maximum number of models that can be bought so that the arrangement is beautiful. You have to answer many queries.
shrine.input: The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of queries. Each query consists of two lines. The first contains an integer $n$, the number of models. The second contains $n$ integers $s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n$, the sizes of the models.
shrine.output: Print $t$ lines. The $i$-th line contains the maximum number of models that can be bought in the $i$-th query.
shrine.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 100$
$1 \le n \le 100000$
$1 \le s_i \le 10^9$
The sum of $n$ over all queries does not exceed $100000$.

shuffle-8.name: Shuffle
shuffle-8.statement:
You are given an array of $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$. Initially $a_x = 1$ and all other elements are $0$.

You must perform $m$ operations. In the $i$-th operation, you choose two indices $c$ and $d$ such that $l_i \le c, d \le r_i$, and swap $a_c$ and $a_d$ (it is allowed that $c = d$).

Calculate the number of indices $k$ such that it is possible to choose the operations so that $a_k = 1$ at the end.
shuffle-8.input: The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases. Each test case starts with a line containing three integers $n$, $x$ and $m$. Each of the next $m$ lines contains two integers $l_i$ and $r_i$, describing the $i$-th operation.
shuffle-8.output: For each test case, print one integer: the number of indices $k$ such that $a_k = 1$ is achievable after all operations.
shuffle-8.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 100$

$1 \le n \le 10^9$

$1 \le x \le n$

$1 \le m \le 100$

$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le n$

brain-rot-outbreak.name: Brain Rot Outbreak
brain-rot-outbreak.statement:
A mysterious disease called Brain Rot is spreading through a village of $n$ houses placed on a circle and numbered $1$ to $n$. House $i$ neighbours house $i+1$ for $1 \le i \le n-1$, and house $n$ neighbours house $1$. Initially $m$ houses are infected.

Each day, the following happens in order:

Cirno chooses an uninfected house and protects it permanently. A protected house can never be infected.
Every uninfected, unprotected house with at least one infected neighbour becomes infected.

Cirno acts optimally to stop Brain Rot from spreading. Find the minimum possible number of infected houses at the end. You must answer $t$ independent test cases.
brain-rot-outbreak.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.
For each test case:

The first line contains two integers $n$ and $m$.
The second line contains $m$ distinct integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m$, the indices of the initially infected houses.
brain-rot-outbreak.output: For each test case, print one integer on its own line: the minimum number of infected houses at the end.
brain-rot-outbreak.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 10^4$

$5 \le n \le 10^9$

$1 \le m \le \min(n, 10^5)$

$1 \le a_i \le n$, all $a_i$ distinct

The sum of $m$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^5$.

roshan-makes-them-equal.name: Roshan Makes Them Equal
roshan-makes-them-equal.statement:
Roshan the wizard has a string $s_1 s_2 \ldots s_n$ and a favourite character $c$. He wants every character of the string to become $c$ using as few spells as possible.

In one spell, Roshan chooses a number $x$ ($1 \le x \le n$) and, for every position $i$ that is not divisible by $x$, replaces $s_i$ with $c$.

Find the minimum number of spells needed to make all characters equal to $c$, and the values of $x$ that Roshan should use, in the order he casts them. It can be proved that an answer always exists under the given constraints. If there are multiple answers, print any of them. You must answer $t$ independent test cases.
roshan-makes-them-equal.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.
For each test case:

The first line contains an integer $n$ and a lowercase Latin letter $c$.
The second line contains a string $s$ of $n$ lowercase Latin letters.
roshan-makes-them-equal.output: For each test case, first print an integer $m$, the minimum number of spells. If $m > 0$, print a second line with $m$ integers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m$ ($1 \le x_j \le n$), the values to use in order. If there are multiple answers, print any.
roshan-makes-them-equal.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 10^4$
$3 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$
$s$ and $c$ consist of lowercase Latin letters.
The sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $3 \cdot 10^5$.

sudhan-and-the-demodogs.name: Sudhan and the Demodogs
sudhan-and-the-demodogs.statement:
Demodogs from the Upside-down have attacked Hawkins again. Sudhan is helping El reach Mike while killing as many Demodogs as possible on the way.

Hawkins is an $n \times n$ grid. The cell in row $i$ and column $j$ contains $i \cdot j$ Demodogs. El starts at $(1,1)$ and must reach $(n,n)$. She can only move right, from $(i,j)$ to $(i,j+1)$, or down, from $(i,j)$ to $(i+1,j)$, and she cannot leave the grid. She kills all Demodogs in every cell she visits, including the start and the finish.

Let $ans$ be the maximum number of Demodogs she can kill. Print $2022 \cdot ans$ modulo $10^9+7$. Multiply by $2022$ first, and only then take the remainder. You must answer $t$ independent test cases.
sudhan-and-the-demodogs.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.
Each of the next $t$ lines contains a single integer $n$, the size of the grid.
sudhan-and-the-demodogs.output: For each test case, print one integer: $2022 \cdot ans \bmod (10^9+7)$.

deja-vu-1-3.name: Deja Vu
deja-vu-1-3.statement:
You are given an array $a$ of $n$ positive integers and an array $x$ of $q$ positive integers. There are $q$ modifications. In the $i$-th modification ($1 \le i \le q$), for every $j$ ($1 \le j \le n$) such that $a_j$ is divisible by $2^{x_i}$, add $2^{x_i - 1}$ to $a_j$. Each $x_i$ is a positive integer not exceeding $30$.

The modifications are applied one after another, in the given order. After all $q$ modifications, output the final array. You must answer $t$ independent test cases.
deja-vu-1-3.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.
For each test case:

The first line contains two integers $n$ and $q$.
The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$.
The third line contains $q$ integers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_q$.
deja-vu-1-3.output: For each test case, print $n$ integers on one line: the array after all modifications.
deja-vu-1-3.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 10^4$
$1 \le n, q \le 10^5$
$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$
$1 \le x_i \le 30$
The sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.
The sum of $q$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.

utsav-and-the-monster-horde.name: Utsav and the Monster Horde
utsav-and-the-monster-horde.statement:
Utsav the brave knight is defending his village from a horde of $n$ monsters, numbered $1$ to $n$. The $i$-th monster has $a_i$ health points.

His enchanted sword has one ability: each time he uses it, it deals $k$ damage to the monster with the highest current health. If several monsters share the highest health, the one with the smaller index is hit. A monster whose health becomes $\le 0$ dies.

Utsav keeps using the ability until every monster is dead. The villagers want to know the order in which the monsters die so they can prepare memorials. Help them by printing the indices of the monsters in the order of their death. You must answer $t$ independent test cases.
utsav-and-the-monster-horde.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.
For each test case:

The first line contains two integers $n$ and $k$.
The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$.
utsav-and-the-monster-horde.output: For each test case, print $n$ integers on one line: the indices of the monsters in the order in which they die.
utsav-and-the-monster-horde.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 10^4$
$1 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$
$1 \le k \le 10^9$
$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$
The sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $3 \cdot 10^5$.

prajwal-and-the-marble-ap.name: Prajwal and the Marble AP
prajwal-and-the-marble-ap.statement: Prajwal loves arranging his marbles in neat rows. He has three piles with $a$, $b$ and $c$ marbles, kept in this order. He wants the piles to form an arithmetic progression, meaning $b-a=c-b$. Before the school bell rings he can perform exactly one magic trick: choose a positive integer $m$ and multiply exactly one of the three piles by $m$ ($m=1$ is allowed). He cannot change the order of the piles. Determine whether Prajwal can make $a, b, c$ form an arithmetic progression. The common difference may be negative or zero. You must answer $t$ independent test cases.
prajwal-and-the-marble-ap.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.
Each of the next $t$ lines contains three integers $a$, $b$ and $c$.
prajwal-and-the-marble-ap.output: For each test case, print “YES” if Prajwal can make the piles form an arithmetic progression, otherwise print “NO”. The answer is case-insensitive.

sunits-permutation-factory.name: Sunit’s Permutation Factory
sunits-permutation-factory.statement:
Sunit runs a Permutation Factory, a machine shop that rearranges arrays. He has two permutations $p$ and $q$ of length $n$. In one operation, he picks two indices $i \ne j$ and swaps $p_i$ and $p_j$, paying a cost of $\min(|i-j|,\ |p_i-p_j|)$.

Find the minimum total cost to make $p_i = q_i$ for all $1 \le i \le n$, and output a sequence of operations that achieves it.

A permutation of length $n$ contains every integer from $1$ to $n$ exactly once.
sunits-permutation-factory.input:
The first line contains an integer $t$, the number of test cases.

Each test case consists of three lines:

The first line contains an integer $n$.
The second line contains $n$ integers $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$.
The third line contains $n$ integers $q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n$.
sunits-permutation-factory.output:
For each test case, print an integer $k$ ($0 \le k \le n^2$), the number of operations. Then print $k$ lines, each with two integers $i, j$ ($1 \le i, j \le n$, $i \ne j$), meaning swap $p_i$ and $p_j$, in order.

The total cost of the operations must be the minimum possible. If several optimal sequences exist, print any of them.Graph Matching, Constructive Algorithms, Min-Cost Matching, Hungarian Algorithm, Greedy
sunits-permutation-factory.constraints:
$1 \le t \le 10^4$

$2 \le n \le 100$

$1 \le p_i, q_i \le n$, and both $p$ and $q$ are permutations

The sum of $n^3$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^6$
